title: Unit 9: Parametric Equations, Polar Coordinates, and Vector-Valued Functions

topics.name: Parametric and vector derivatives and arc length
covers: Finding derivatives of parametric functions and vector-valued functions
Calculating the accumulation of change in length over an interval using a definite integral

topics.name: Motion in the plane
covers: Determining the position of a particle moving in a plane
Calculating velocity, speed, and acceleration of a particle moving along a curve

topics.name: Polar derivatives and area
covers: Finding derivatives of functions written in polar coordinates
Finding the area of regions bounded by polar curves

guide.title: Parametric, polar, and vector-valued functions: review guide
guide.intro: This BC-only unit describes curves with a parameter, with vectors, and in polar coordinates. It finds slopes, lengths, motion in the plane, and areas inside polar curves.

sections.title: Parametric and vector derivatives and arc length
body: For x = x(t), y = y(t): dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). The second derivative is d²y/dx² = (d/dt of dy/dx)/(dx/dt): differentiate dy/dx with respect to t, then divide by dx/dt again.
The length of a parametric curve from t = a to t = b is ∫ from a to b of √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt. A vector-valued function r(t) = ⟨x(t), y(t)⟩ differentiates component by component.
points: Horizontal tangent: dy/dt = 0 (with dx/dt ≠ 0). Vertical tangent: dx/dt = 0 (with dy/dt ≠ 0).
Don't forget the second division by dx/dt in d²y/dx².
Arc length counts any retraced part of the path again.

sections.title: Motion in the plane
body: For position r(t) = ⟨x(t), y(t)⟩: velocity v(t) = ⟨x′(t), y′(t)⟩, acceleration a(t) = ⟨x″(t), y″(t)⟩, and speed |v(t)| = √(x′² + y′²).
Position at time b = position at time a + ∫ from a to b of v(t) dt, component by component. The distance traveled is ∫ speed dt, which is usually more than the straight-line displacement.
points: Speed is a number; velocity is a vector.
Add the initial position to each component.
Distance traveled uses the speed, not the separate components.

sections.title: Polar derivatives and area
body: For r = f(θ), use x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ as parametric equations in θ: dy/dx = (dy/dθ)/(dx/dθ), with dy/dθ = r′ sin θ + r cos θ and dx/dθ = r′ cos θ − r sin θ.
The area swept out by r = f(θ) from θ = α to θ = β is (1/2) ∫ from α to β of r² dθ. For the area between two polar curves, use (1/2) ∫ (R² − r²) dθ.
points: dr/dθ is not the slope of the curve: it's the rate at which the distance from the origin changes.
Find the θ-limits where r = 0 or where the curves intersect.
Use symmetry, such as one petal times the number of petals, carefully.

example.prompt: For x = t², y = t³ − 3t, where does the curve have a horizontal tangent?
example.solution: dy/dt = 3t² − 3 = 0 at t = ±1, and dx/dt = 2t ≠ 0 there. The points are (1, −2) at t = 1 and (1, 2) at t = −1.

misconceptions: “d²y/dx² is the derivative of dy/dx with respect to t.”
That result must be divided by dx/dt again.
“dr/dθ is the slope of a polar curve.”
The slope is dy/dx, using x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ.

questions.prompt: For x = t² and y = t³, what is dy/dx at t = 2?
choiceExplanations: 4 is dx/dt at t = 2.
1/3 is dx/dy, the reciprocal.
12 is dy/dt at t = 2, not dy/dx.

questions.prompt: For x = t² and y = t³ (t > 0), what is d²y/dx²?
questions.explanation: dy/dx = 3t/2. Differentiate with respect to t to get 3/2, then divide by dx/dt = 2t: 3/(4t).
choiceExplanations: 3/(2t) divides by t instead of by dx/dt = 2t.
3t/2 is the first derivative dy/dx.
3/2 forgets to divide by dx/dt.

questions.prompt: What is the length of the path x = 3 cos t, y = 3 sin t for 0 ≤ t ≤ π?
questions.explanation: √((−3 sin t)² + (3 cos t)²) = 3, so L = ∫ from 0 to π of 3 dt = 3π: half a circle of radius 3.
choiceExplanations: 3 is the speed, not multiplied by the time interval π.
9π/2 is the area of the half-disc, not a length.
6π is the full circle's circumference; t only goes to π.

questions.prompt: A particle's position is r(t) = ⟨t², 4t⟩. What is its speed at t = 1?
choiceExplanations: 6 adds the components instead of using the Pythagorean theorem.
√17 is the distance from the origin to the position ⟨1, 4⟩.
20 is the speed squared.

questions.prompt: A particle has velocity v(t) = ⟨2t, 3⟩ and position ⟨1, −2⟩ at t = 0. Where is it at t = 2?
questions.explanation: Integrate each component from 0 to 2: Δx = 4 and Δy = 6. Add them to the start: ⟨1 + 4, −2 + 6⟩ = ⟨5, 4⟩.
choiceExplanations: ⟨4, 6⟩ is the displacement; it forgets the starting position.
⟨4, 3⟩ is the velocity at t = 2.
⟨5, 1⟩ adds the velocity's y-component (3) instead of its integral (6).

questions.prompt: A particle's position is r(t) = ⟨sin t, t³⟩. What is its acceleration at t = π/2?
choiceExplanations: The second derivative of sin t is −sin t, so the x-component is −1.
⟨0, 3π²/4⟩ is the velocity ⟨cos t, 3t²⟩ at π/2.
6 is the y-component's third derivative, not 6t evaluated at π/2.

questions.prompt: A particle starts at the origin with velocity v(t) = ⟨2t, t²⟩. What distance does it travel from t = 0 to t = 2?
questions.explanation: Speed = √(4t² + t⁴) = t√(4 + t²). Distance = ∫ from 0 to 2 of t√(4 + t²) dt = (1/3)(4 + t²)^(3/2) from 0 to 2 = (16√2 − 8)/3.
choiceExplanations: 4√2 is the speed at t = 2.
20/3 adds the two components' displacements, 4 + 8/3.
√208/3 is the straight-line distance to the end point ⟨4, 8/3⟩; the path curves.

questions.prompt: What is the area enclosed by the polar curve r = 2 sin θ for 0 ≤ θ ≤ π?
questions.explanation: A = (1/2) ∫ from 0 to π of 4 sin²θ dθ = 2 · (π/2) = π. (The curve is a circle of radius 1.)
choiceExplanations: 2π forgets the 1/2 in the polar area formula.
4π uses r = 2 as if it were a circle of radius 2.
π/2 is half the correct area.

questions.prompt: For the polar curve r = 1 + cos θ, what is dy/dx at θ = π/2?
questions.explanation: dy/dθ = r′ sin θ + r cos θ = −sin²θ + (1 + cos θ)cos θ = −1 at π/2. dx/dθ = r′ cos θ − r sin θ = −1 at π/2. So dy/dx = (−1)/(−1) = 1.
choiceExplanations: dy/dθ isn't 0 at π/2, so the tangent isn't horizontal.
dx/dθ = −1 isn't 0, so the slope is defined.
−1 is dr/dθ = −sin θ at π/2, not the slope dy/dx.

questions.prompt: What is the area of one petal of the rose r = cos(2θ)?
questions.explanation: One petal runs from θ = −π/4 to π/4. A = (1/2) ∫ from −π/4 to π/4 of cos²(2θ) dθ = (1/2)(π/4) = π/8.
choiceExplanations: π/2 is the area of all four petals.
π/4 forgets the 1/2 in the polar area formula.
1/2 integrates r instead of r².
